intro: Delhi is India's capital, a city of Mughal tombs, gardens and wide green lawns among the traffic. Near Humayun's Tomb a reader found two great figs about 300 metres apart and sent us their photographs: a peepal, the sacred fig of India, with a vast rounded crown over a trunk of fused stems on a stone plinth, and a banyan whose hanging roots have grown into pillars beside an arcaded Mughal pavilion. We do not yet know their ages.

trees.story:
A reader sent us this tree from a garden of lawns and stone water channels near Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, and called it a Bodhi tree.

It is a peepal, Ficus religiosa, the fig under which the Buddha is said to have found enlightenment and a tree sacred to Hindus and Jains as well, which is why so many of them are left to grow old across India. This one has had room to do it. In the reader's first photograph the crown is a huge rounded mass, wider than it is tall, and the people picnicking on the grass beneath it look tiny. The trunk sits on a raised stone plinth, short and enormously thick, made of many grey stems and roots that have grown together.

The second photograph stands under the branches. The heart-shaped leaves, each drawn out into a long thin tip, hang so thick they hide the sky, and across the lawn an old domed building rises behind arcaded walls.

We do not know its age, its girth or who planted it. If you know this tree, tell us here and we will add what you know.

Sit on the plinth's edge in the afternoon, when the lawn fills with people.

trees.story:
A reader sent us this banyan from a garden of lawns and paths a few minutes' walk from Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, and named it an Indian Banyan.

A banyan, Ficus benghalensis, is India's national tree, and it grows in a way no other tree does. Its branches let down thin roots that hang in the air until they reach the soil, then thicken into new trunks, so an old banyan slowly turns into a grove that is still one tree. This one is well on its way. In the reader's photograph the trunk is not one stem but a bundle of pale roots grown into pillars, and the long limbs reach out sideways far over the paths, the broad leathery leaves hanging thick enough to shade everyone walking below.

Behind it stands an old building of white cusped arches set in red walls, Mughal in style, so close that the banyan seems to lean against its arcade. People stroll the paths and sit on the grass under the outer branches.

We do not know its age, its girth or who planted it. If you know this tree, tell us here and we will add what you know.

It stands about 300 metres from The Peepal on the Plinth, our other Delhi tree, so the two make a short walk.
